In contrast, certain parsing algorithms, such as LKE, exhibit $O(n^2)$ time complexity, which renders them incapable of processing large datasets in a reasonable time [2].

The efficiency of some tree-based methods relies on simplifying assumptions; for example, LeafRefit’s efficiency derives from the assumption that instance deletions do not affect the trees’ structure [3].

Additionally, pruning strategies can be introduced during tree construction to eliminate interference from query-irrelevant nodes, as seen in hypothesis tree building for temporal sentence localization [4].
Succinct representations of static ordinal trees can support a variety of navigation operations, including level-ancestor, in $O(1)$ time on the RAM model while using $2n + o(n)$ bits of space [5].

Similarly, the range min-max tree data structure reduces a large number of relevant tree operations to a few primitives that are carried out in constant time on polylog-sized trees, extending to trees of arbitrary size while retaining constant time [6].
These succinct representations are within $o(n)$ bits of the information-theoretic minimum for representing an $n$-node tree [5].
The underlying indexable dictionaries used in these structures support rank and select operations in $O(1)$ time on the RAM model [7][8].
The range min-max tree achieves a space complexity of $2n + O(n/\text{polylog}(n))$ bits, which is optimal for a core subset of operations and significantly lower than previous proposals [6].
In the context of suffix trees, which are critical in bioinformatics, recent research has obtained various compressed representations with widely different space-time tradeoffs [9].
The use of range min-max trees in suffix tree representations yields novel practical space/time tradeoffs and allows for the indexing of highly repetitive collections [9].

Conversely, opportunistic data structures achieve space occupancy that is a function of the entropy of the underlying data set, decreasing space when input is compressible at no significant slowdown in query performance [10].
Specifically, such structures allow searching for occurrences of a pattern $P$ in text $T$ in $O(p + \text{occ} \log^\epsilon u)$ time [10].

For example, extracting maximal disconnected principal submatrices in poset-related analyses requires $O(n^4)$ time, remaining tractable for specific sizes where backtracking algorithms time out [11].

Furthermore, the complexity of encoding and decoding in general data compression models, which include macro schemes based on finding redundant strings, is a subject of discussion regarding trade-offs between compression amount and algorithmic cost [13].
In deep learning, XGBoost provides insights into cache access patterns and data compression to build a scalable tree boosting system, scaling beyond billions of examples using fewer resources [14].
However, in high-dimensional spaces, K-D trees can degenerate into linear search due to sparse data distribution, impacting query efficiency [15].

For geometric compression, efficient compression and decompression algorithms for triangulated models aim to reduce transmission time and storage space, though the specific time complexity for the topological surgery is not explicitly quantified in the excerpt [16].

In the context of graphical models, the sample complexity of the SGA algorithm for partial recovery of tree-structured models is significantly better than that of the algorithm by Katiyar et al. [17].

Similarly, in neural network compression, Huffman coding is noted as the most efficient method for encoding scattered data due to its optimal compression rate, but its complexity makes it difficult to employ due to computation-hungry compressor/decompressor schemes [20].

The range min-max tree data structure is extended to the dynamic case, where insertion and deletion operations are supported, although the specific time complexity for these dynamic operations is not fully detailed in the provided excerpt beyond the mention of the extension [6].

The choice of data structure, such as the row-binary forest inspired by Fenwick trees, is proposed to encode edge-binary trees, indicating a specific structural approach to managing tree data [21].

Overall, the computational cost of building and querying compressed trees varies from polynomial time for construction in some algorithms to constant time for queries in succinct static representations, with significant trade-offs in space usage and implementation complexity [6][1][5].

In the context of database indexing, B-trees have become the de facto standard for file organization, with their success attributed to a careful contrast of the relative merits and costs of various implementations, such as the B+-tree [1].

However, this balance is not uniform across all dimensions; for instance, K-D trees, which are effective in lower dimensions, degenerate into linear search in higher dimensions due to sparse data distribution, indicating a significant increase in time complexity as dimensionality grows [2].

Similarly, in high-dimensional feature spaces used for multimedia retrieval, query processing requires navigating complex similarity searches that transform content-based retrieval into point searches, where the efficiency of the underlying structure dictates the overall system performance [3].

For example, in the domain of parse trees, simplifying inessential parts such as parentheses by implying information through hierarchy reduces the structural complexity, effectively trading explicit storage for implicit structural inference [4].

This approach aligns with broader compression strategies where reducing space impacts the ability to perform efficient lookups; in medical document summarization, a compression ratio of only 10 is observed for specific token types compared to a ratio of 45 for all tokens, highlighting that the granularity of compression directly affects the resulting data size and potentially the retrieval fidelity [5].

The choice of representation is critical, as switching from a naive representation to a compact codebook significantly improves matters for alphabets with a large number of symbols, such as words, thereby optimizing the space-time balance for large-scale text compression [6].

Conversely, in federated recommendation systems, the reduction of communication costs through model compression sacrifices the computation resources of the clients, necessitating a careful consideration of the trade-off between computation and communication costs [8].

This dynamic is also evident in image compression, where learned frameworks may use static compression and decompression models fixed after training, which prevents efficient rate-distortion optimization and thus limits the ability to dynamically adjust the space-time trade-off based on real-time requirements [9].

For instance, in system log parsing, algorithms such as SLCT, Paddy, Lenma, and LogCluster are sensitive to preprocessing, with variations in this phase affecting up to 10% of the overall performance, indicating that the initial structuring of data into tree-like or clustered formats has a measurable impact on efficiency [10].

Similarly, in the analysis of tree ring data, the use of Random Forest methods yields accurate results with the lowest Root Mean Square Error, but the computational cost of training such ensemble models must be considered against the accuracy gains [11].

In the context of dynamic least-squares regression, sharp separations exist between the amortized update times of fully versus partially dynamic settings, showing that the level of dynamism and accuracy required directly dictates the computational complexity of maintaining the underlying data structures [12].

Reducing isomorphism testing to a sequence of structured tree comparisons rather than an explicit search over permutations offers a more efficient pathway, although fast canonicalization remains a natural but currently missing preprocessing step in many workflows [13].

In the domain of graph generation, data structures like the row-binary forest, inspired by Fenwick trees, are proposed to encode edge-binary trees, aiming to optimize the storage and retrieval of generated structures [14].

Furthermore, in temporal sentence localization, pruning strategies are introduced during tree construction to eliminate query-irrelevant nodes, which reduces the search space and thereby improves query execution time at the cost of potential information loss [15].

Multi-component key indexes, for example, can improve average query execution time by up to 130 times for high-frequency word queries, demonstrating that specific indexing structures can drastically reduce time complexity for certain query patterns [16].

In contrast, caching policies, such as those used in ATRAPOS for metapath query workloads, select intermediate results to cache and reuse by detecting frequent sub-metapaths using an Overlap Tree, which trades storage space for reduced computation time in real-time evaluation [17].
These examples underscore that the optimal balance between space and time is highly dependent on the specific workload, data distribution, and the nature of the queries being executed.

In the context of medical document summarization, specific compression methods have been observed to achieve a compression ratio of only 10, which stands in stark contrast to the compression ratio of 45 achieved when processing all tokens [1].
This discrepancy highlights that the choice of algorithm and the granularity of the data being compressed directly impact the efficiency of the reduction process.

Similarly, in the domain of prompt compression for large language models, empirical distinctions are drawn between Text-to-Vector (T2V) and Text-to-Text (T2T) approaches, where T2V treats the model as a compressor for vector representations, while T2T directly measures token informativeness to remove redundancy [2].

The effectiveness of these methods is often constrained by the underlying representation of the data; for instance, in single text compression, switching from a naive codebook representation to a compact one significantly improves performance, particularly for alphabets with a large number of symbols such as words [3].

Consequently, accurate evaluation of compression performance requires accounting for the full code length, which includes both the length of the encoded text and the length of the codebook itself [3].
Neural networks are characterized as both computationally and memory intensive, making their deployment on embedded systems with limited hardware resources difficult [4].

To mitigate this, the "deep compression" pipeline employs pruning, trained quantization, and Huffman coding to reduce storage requirements by 35x to 49x without affecting accuracy, with pruning alone reducing the number of connections by 9x to 13x [4].

In the realm of 3-D geometric compression, the need to reduce the memory or disk space required to store complex triangulated models has driven the development of schemes that quantize vertex positions and utilize vertex spanning trees [5].

Furthermore, in the context of approximate algorithms for maximum inner product search, systems like Sinnamon offer levers to trade-off memory consumption, latency, and accuracy, making them suitable for constrained applications [6].

The practical aspects of using data compression for prefetching in database systems also involve analyzing the I/O involved in moving objects from slow memory to cache, where prefetchers based on Lempel-Ziv data compressors have been shown to be theoretically optimal in the limit [7].

While tree boosting is a highly effective method, systems like XGBoost require specific insights on cache access patterns, data compression, and sharding to scale beyond billions of examples using fewer resources than existing systems [8].
In contrast, many deep graph generation methods, despite their goal of being used on real-world applications such as social network graphs, suffer from scalability issues [9].

This limitation is not unique to graph generation; scalability issues also limit the applicability of manifold learning methods for handling large-scale data [10], and researchers have focused on inductive reasoning models for knowledge graphs due to scalability and expressive ability issues in previous approaches [11].
The computational scalability of methods for large posets, which involve reducing isomorphism testing to structured tree comparisons, remains to be systematically evaluated [12].
Additionally, parameter-centric approaches in recommender systems lack scalability and flexibility, as the capacity is hard to scale and the knowledge is inflexible to utilize [13].

In time series classification, previous evaluations made comparisons between algorithms difficult due to the use of different programming languages, single train/test splits, and inconsistent data normalization practices [14].
To address this, a common Java framework was implemented to evaluate 18 recently proposed algorithms against standard baselines on an expanded archive of 85 datasets [14].

Similarly, in the field of systematic reviews and meta-analyses, poor reporting of key information has diminished the value of these studies for clinicians and policy makers, leading to the development of guidelines like PRISMA to improve clarity and transparency [15][16].

In the context of privacy-preserving model explanations, greedy algorithms for constructing decision trees select features based on Gini impurity, allowing for the identification and discarding of attribute combinations that do not contribute to an optimal tree [17].

However, the estimation of performance without data compression serves as an upper bound of the real scenario, indicating that empirical results must account for the overhead of compression techniques to be realistic [18].

Tree transformations are used to organize document content into a logical tree structure to aid in categorization and extraction, but the effectiveness of these structures depends on the logical coherence of the source material [19].

In financial applications, market microstructure poses challenges to volatility estimation from high-frequency data, where the "usual" volatility estimator fails when returns are sampled at the highest frequency [20].

For global land data assimilation, systems like GLDAS must ingest satellite and ground-based observational data to generate optimal fields of land surface states, requiring the integration of a huge quantity of observation-based data at high resolution [21].

The rapid evolution of big data has forced the academic press to catch up with industry adoption, highlighting the need for efficient analytic methods for unstructured data, which constitutes 95% of big data [22].

In the domain of explainable AI, tree ensembles aim to overcome poor performance by aggregating predictions from trees learned on different subsets of training data, yet the scalability of such ensemble methods remains a concern [23].

Finally, while gradient-based learning techniques like back-propagation are successful for synthesizing complex decision surfaces, real-life document recognition systems are composed of multiple modules including field extraction, segmentation, and language modeling, indicating that tree-based or compression algorithms must integrate within broader pipelines [24].

data.question: Are there papers that use different formats of Q&A with the user to clarify intent and compose more complicated prompts to LLM?

data.response:
The primary objective of interactive prompting strategies is to resolve the inherent ambiguity in natural language, a challenge that persists even as models scale [1]. While scaling alone may not overcome issues where a source query yields multiple valid options without extra context, interactive methods aim to reduce these ambiguities before final execution [1]. A fundamental limitation of static prompting is that making language models bigger does not inherently make them better at following a user’s intent [2]. Consequently, researchers have developed various frameworks to disambiguate user intent through clarification, iterative refinement, and structured reasoning elicitation.

One category of strategies involves the direct generation of clarification questions to resolve misunderstandings. In open-domain settings, models can be trained to produce polar (yes-no) clarification questions to resolve uncertainty in dialogue, using an expected information gain objective to derive informative questions without requiring supervised question-answer data [3]. This approach mirrors the human process of "repair," where questions are asked until uncertainty is resolved [3]. In specific domains such as robotic object disambiguation, few-shot prompt engineering systems have been developed to improve the LLM's ability to pose disambiguating queries [4]. Similarly, in crosslingual conditional generation, "interactive-chain prompting" introduces a series of question, answering, and generation intermediate steps between a Translator model and a User model [1]. This method reduces translations into a list of subproblems addressing ambiguities, resolving them before producing the final text [1].

Another significant approach is iterative refinement, where the prompt or the model's output is revised based on feedback. Self-refine has verified that LLMs possess the competency for iterative refinement across various tasks based on self-feedback, leading many optimized prompting frameworks to include iterative feedback loops [5]. In the context of deployed models like GPT-3, memory-assisted prompt editing pairs the model with a growing memory of recorded cases where it misunderstood user intents, along with user feedback for clarification [6]. This memory allows the system to produce enhanced prompts for new queries based on past error corrections, substantially increasing accuracy over queries with different kinds of misunderstandings [6]. For developers, tools like EvalLM provide an interactive system for iteratively refining prompts by evaluating multiple outputs on user-defined criteria, helping participants compose more diverse criteria and examine outputs more thoroughly than manual evaluation [7]. Furthermore, reinforcement learning-driven query refinement frameworks refine user prompts before they are input into LLMs to improve the quality of queries and ensure responses are truthful and benign [8].

Chain-of-thought (CoT) elicitation and related reasoning structures represent another major category of interactive prompting strategies. Task-specific prompting, such as zero-shot Chain-of-Thought, is a standard method for enhancing reasoning capabilities [9]. More sophisticated prompting strategies include Chain of Thought (CoT), Tree of Thought (ToT), and Graph of Thought (GoT), which allow large language models to address complex tasks effectively [10]. Self-consistency, a technique compatible with other ensemble strategies, improves chain-of-thought reasoning by sampling multiple reasoning paths and selecting the most consistent answer, with gains significantly higher than other ensemble strategies [11]. This method is robust to various sampling strategies and parameters [11]. In the domain of prompt engineering, "λ prompt" allows for building complete large LM-based prompt machines, including ones that self-edit to correct and even self-write their own execution code [12].

Several systems integrate these strategies into multi-stage pipelines to extract and correct user intent. In infrastructure-as-code generation, LLMs extract user intent, send it to an intent corrector that confirms, corrects, and converts it into JSON, and updates intents [13]. Tools like Infracopilot use LLMs to understand user intent to revolutionize cloud infrastructure development [13]. In multimodal search, the CUE-M framework addresses challenges in interpreting user intent through a multi-stage pipeline comprising image context enrichment, intent refinement, contextual query generation, and relevance-based filtering [14]. For recommendation systems, Reinforced Prompt Personalization (RPP) introduces instance-wise prompting to personalize discrete prompts for individual users, breaking down prompts at the sentence level to improve efficiency and quality [15].

Despite these advancements, automatic prompt engineering significantly alleviates human labor but still cannot completely avoid human intervention [5]. Many methods focus on improving the quality of the prompt in a single stage, but more advanced techniques such as prompt engineering, label words engineering, prompt pre-training, and prompt ensembling are orthogonal and can further improve performance [16]. The integration of these interactive methods is crucial because deep generative models, while promising for end-users, are often hard to control without such prompting mechanisms [17]. By composing prompts and using interactive evaluation, developers can prototype novel generative applications and refine them into products by diagnosing weaknesses in outputs [7].

Architectures for multi-turn intent clarification often rely on decomposing complex user requests into manageable sub-tasks to facilitate precise interaction. LLMs can decompose complex tasks down into sub-tasks to assist agents in planning over longer temporal horizons, aiding in the decision-making process for complex, multi-step tasks [1]. This decomposition is frequently achieved through step-by-step reasoning that progressively retrieves relevant nodes from a graph, allowing for the handling of intricate task structures [2]. Adding chain-of-thoughts can effectively decompose complex reasoning tasks into intermediate reasoning steps, which serves as a foundational mechanism for these architectures [3]. In the context of retrieval-augmented generation, complex queries may require multi-step retrieval where relevant evidence is fetched from one or a small subset of possible sources, necessitating an interleaving of reasoning and retrieval steps [4].

Specific frameworks have been developed to operationalize these multi-turn interactions. The RAISE (Reasoning and Acting through Scratchpad and Examples) architecture enhances the integration of Large Language Models into conversational agents [5]. Similarly, the MixAlign framework interacts with the user to get clarification when the LLM is uncertain about its mapping from the user query to the database [6]. In the domain of conversational recommendation, tool-augmented LLMs focus on architecture design for LLM-driven control of dialogue, recommender modules, and external reasoners, with a specific emphasis on methods for proactive conversational recommendation [7]. Reprompting ChatGPT with feedback has been identified as an effective strategy to improve recommendation relevancy, indicating a multi-turn refinement process [8].

The challenge of maintaining context and resolving ambiguity in multi-turn settings remains significant. It is challenging to address the ellipsis and resolution problem in a multi-turn setting, particularly in hybrid question-answering scenarios [9]. Related Pre-trained Language Model (PrLM) models commonly represent dialogues sequentially by processing the pairwise dialogue history as a whole, which means hierarchical information on utterance interrelation or speaker roles is not well addressed [10]. To mitigate this, the Channel-aware Decoupling Network was proposed, and experimental results show that this method substantially boosts strong PrLM baselines in four public benchmark datasets, achieving new state-of-the-art performance over previous methods [10]. Furthermore, a benchmark called SAMSum, a human-annotated dataset specifically designed for multi-turn dialogue summarization, has been proposed to evaluate the quality of dialogue summaries generated by LLMs via In-Context Learning [3].

Agent-based architectures extend these capabilities by incorporating memory and strategic planning. Generative agents utilize an architecture that extends a large language model to store a complete record of the agent’s experiences using natural language, synthesize those memories over time into higher-level reflections, and retrieve them dynamically to plan behavior [11]. In the initialization of an LLM-based agent participant, a system message is required for configuration, commonly including persona setting, target alignment, and functionality declaration [12]. The reasoning mechanism in such agents defines how the LLM generates reasoning traces, such as plans, explanations, or self-critiques, that guide action proposals [13]. A unified framework for LLM-based autonomous agents has been proposed to encompass much of the previous work, discussing the construction of these agents from a holistic perspective [14].

In specialized domains, these architectures are adapted to specific workflow requirements. In chemistry, an LLM agent has been developed that is capable of automatically completing complex planning and synthesis tasks, although the emergent abilities of LLMs in complex molecular tasks have not been fully shown [15]. For production systems, a novel approach integrates LLM agents into automated production systems by organizing operations within a hierarchical framework based on the automation pyramid, where atomic operation functionalities are modeled as microservices [16]. Upon receiving a user request or identifying a triggering event, these LLM agents generate a process plan, with low-level hardware-specific data semantically enriched and made interpretable for the LLMs [16]. In the domain of collaborative AI system design, ComfyAgent is a framework that empowers LLM-based agents to autonomously design collaborative AI systems by generating workflows, representing these workflows with code that can be reversibly converted [17].

The role of human-in-the-loop workflows and strategic reasoning is also integral to these architectures. Iterated decomposition is described as a human-in-the-loop workflow for developing and refining compositional LM programs [18]. While automatic prompt engineering significantly alleviates human labor, it still cannot completely avoid human intervention [9]. Strategic reasoning with LLMs involves task-specific prompting, such as zero-shot Chain-of-Thought, to guide the agent's behavior [12]. The concept of World Models has attracted attention in the context of AI agents, intended to help the agent predict the future evolution of environmental states or fill in missing information so that it can plan its actions and behave safely [19].

Historical and foundational architectures provide context for current multi-turn dialogue systems. An architecture for conversational systems was described that enables human-like performance along several levels, involving both general and task-specific knowledge, with generation being incremental and involving phenomena such as turn-taking, grounding, and interruptions [20]. In knowledge acquisition, shared task models have been used as an intermediate representation of a task, with roles including decision support, multi-agent systems for acquisition processes, and designing user interaction at the level of strategic preferences [21]. The Sparrow information-seeking dialogue agent was trained to be more helpful, correct, and harmless by breaking down requirements for good dialogue into natural language rules and asking raters about each rule separately, enabling more targeted human judgements [22].

Other frameworks and surveys highlight the breadth of these applications. ToolLLM is a general tool-use framework that includes ToolBench constructed with an API collection [23]. LLMs can transform diverse and informal natural language information into formal task-specific information, such as feature representation or task-specific languages, thus assisting the learning process of the RL agent [1]. In the context of red teaming, some approaches have included the prompt and formulated the content as a dialogue to test generative models [24]. The prompt machine concept allows for building complete large LM-based prompt machines, including ones that self-edit to correct and even self-write their own execution code [25]. However, there is a gap between optimization objectives in prompt engineering and prompt compression, where the former tends to optimize shorter instructions while the latter mainly deals with longer demonstrations [23]. The LLM Workflow Quadrant is defined by a single load-bearing property where the path is decided in advance, addressing failure modes in autonomous AI agent architectures [26].

The structural integration of clarified intent into final prompts relies on several distinct techniques, ranging from manual template construction to autonomous generation and dynamic chaining. Manual construction is identified as suitable for template-based prompts and few-shot prompting where the prompt structure is uncomplicated, while LM-generated prompts are used to address the shortcomings of manual construction [1]. In contrast, retrieval-based prompts often depend on well-annotated external resources, such as Wikipedia, to alleviate the instability issues associated with pure generation, though this approach consumes expensive information retrieval resources [1]. Beyond static templates, prompt engineering is increasingly viewed as a form of programming that customizes outputs and interactions, with specific patterns serving as reusable solutions to common problems in output generation [2].

A significant area of research focuses on prompt chaining, where the output of one LLM step becomes the input for the next to aggregate gains and handle complex tasks that cannot be resolved in a single run [3][4]. This chaining approach has been shown to improve the quality of task outcomes while significantly enhancing system transparency, controllability, and the user's sense of collaboration [3]. However, authoring these chains requires careful scaffolding for transforming intermediate node outputs and debugging at multiple granularities, which tools like PromptChainer aim to facilitate through visual programming [4]. The concept of chaining is also applied in strategic reasoning, where task-specific prompting, such as zero-shot Chain-of-Thought, is utilized to guide the model through logical steps [5]. Furthermore, backward chaining, which proceeds from a goal to the supporting facts, has been suggested as an alternative to forward chaining in reasoning tasks [6].

Dynamic prompt generation and optimization techniques allow for the adaptation of prompts based on specific instances or continuous feedback. Dynamic prompting frameworks analyze the position, length, and representations of prompts, revealing that optimizing the prompt position to encompass the input can capture semantic information that traditional prefix or postfix methods miss [7]. In the context of black-box tuning, prompts are not necessarily discrete and can be optimized efficiently in continuous space using gradient descent [8]. Autonomous prompt engineering tools, such as the Automatic Prompt Engineering Toolbox (APET), enable models like GPT-4 to autonomously apply prompt engineering techniques to optimize performance on customized tasks [9]. Additionally, reprompting with user feedback has been found to be an effective strategy for improving recommendation relevancy and mitigating popularity bias through prompt engineering [10]. This process involves building a pipeline that simulates realistic user probing by first instructing the model and then reprompting with feedback to refine the output set [10].

In dialogue systems, the integration of clarified intent often involves dynamically updating the dialogue state to elicit specific requirements. A Personalized Utterance Style (PUS) based dialogue strategy chooses suitable response actions for dynamically updating the dialogue state, allowing the system to shrink the search scope of the potential requirement space with the assistance of PUS extracted from dialogue history [11]. This approach is part of a broader trend toward intent-centric, conversation-oriented development, where AI systems evolve beyond task-driven copilots into intelligent collaborators capable of reasoning about software engineering principles and intents [12]. In the domain of human-robot interaction, natural-language dialog is used to express intents and communicate instructions for improvement, enabling robots to learn from interaction experience incrementally and improve their behaviors or avoid future mistakes [13].

The composition of prompts also involves specific structural elements and data handling practices. For instance, in training data construction, prompts may be categorized by type, such as "Basic prompt" where no prefix is added, or by task, such as brainstorming or multiple choice completion [14]. To ensure diversity in use cases, heuristics are applied to deduplicate prompts by checking for those that share a long common prefix [14]. In the context of safety and red teaming, prompt composition is used to modify inputs; for example, when a user inputs a potentially harmful prompt, methods may automatically modify the prompt to ensure generated images are appropriate by retaining acceptable aspects of the original input [15]. Various red-teaming methods, such as Puzzler and GUARD, utilize templates and prompted LLMs with composition or mutation operations to generate adversarial prompts [15].

Other techniques involve the synthesis of prompts for specific multimodal or specialized tasks. In chemistry, LLM agents are capable of automatically completing complex planning and synthesis tasks, representing the first such agent in the field [16]. In image generation, the Prompt Diffusion model introduces a diffusion-based model with in-context learning abilities, guided by an extra text prompt for more precise image generation [17]. In software testing, the automation of test oracles requires knowledge of expected behavior, which may only be known to the developer, highlighting the challenge of integrating this specific intent into automated prompts [18]. In threat modeling for banking systems, frameworks like ThreatModeling-LLM automate processes to enhance efficiency and efficacy, addressing challenges such as the lack of domain-specific datasets and the need for tailored models [19].

The efficacy of these prompt composition techniques is often evaluated through specific benchmarks and datasets. The SAMSum benchmark, a human-annotated dataset for multi-turn dialogue summarization, is used to evaluate the quality of dialogue summaries generated by LLMs via in-context learning [17]. In the context of tool use, ToolLLM is a general framework that includes ToolBench, constructed with an API collection, and ToolLLaMA is supervised fine-tuned by ToolBench [20]. The complexity of prompt construction is also reflected in the scale of data used for training, such as limiting the number of prompts to 200 per user ID or analyzing prompt length distributions in contractor datasets [14]. Furthermore, the use of different sets of prompts, such as x40, has been shown to impact performance metrics in self-consistency reasoning [21]. The integration of persona input in synthesizing dialogues yields utterances with more distinct preferences that are less similar to each other, as observed in the Pearl dataset [22].

Finally, the broader implications of prompt composition relate to the cognitive demands placed on users and the potential for self-editing systems. Generative AI systems impose metacognitive demands on users, requiring a high degree of monitoring and control, which could be addressed by integrating metacognitive support strategies into the systems [23]. The concept of prompt machines extends to systems that can self-edit to correct and even self-write their own execution code, allowing for the building of complete large LM-based prompt machines [1]. In sentiment analysis for conversational agents, user feedback is used to confirm expectations regarding the results obtained from the system [24]. However, challenges remain in knowledge-enhanced dialogue systems, where if the representation does not separate knowledge and dialogue sufficiently, the knowledge may be lost in the output representation, and issues such as dealing with out-of-vocabulary entities persist [25].

Empirical evaluations of clarification strategies in Large Language Models (LLMs) indicate that standard prompting techniques often fail to address user ambiguity, leading to incorrect responses rather than requests for clarification [1]. To address this, the CLAM framework was developed to enable language models to selectively ask for clarification by detecting ambiguity, generating appropriate clarifying questions, and providing final answers after receiving user input [1]. Empirical results show that CLAM significantly improves language model accuracy on mixed ambiguous and unambiguous questions compared to state-of-the-art baselines [1]. This improvement is achieved by simulating users with privileged information, which allows for the automatic evaluation of multi-turn clarification dialogues [1]. Similarly, the MixAlign framework interacts with users to obtain clarification specifically when the LLM is uncertain about its mapping from a user query to a database [2]. In the domain of robotic object disambiguation, a few-shot prompt engineering system has been developed to enhance the LLM's ability to pose disambiguating queries [3].

The effectiveness of clarification questions in engaging users within search systems is currently constrained, casting doubt on their overall usefulness [4]. To improve performance, it is crucial to employ assessment approaches that encompass both real-time user feedback (online evaluation) and human-assessed characteristics of clarification questions (offline evaluation) [4]. However, the relationship between online and offline evaluations has been debated in information retrieval, with studies investigating how offline ranked lists of clarification resemble ideal ranked lists based on online user engagement [4]. In the context of conversational AI, effective ambiguity detection and coreference resolution are key to task success, as referential descriptions do not always uniquely identify the referent [5]. Models such as TOD-BERT and LXMERT have been used to detect ambiguity and resolve coreference, with results showing that language models can exploit data correlations to detect ambiguity [5]. Furthermore, unimodal coreference resolution models can avoid the need for vision in certain contexts [5].

Training LLMs to ask clarifying questions requires specific preference data labeling practices; existing models often presuppose a single interpretation of ambiguous requests because responses are evaluated only on prior contexts [6]. To address this, preference labels can be assigned by simulating expected outcomes in future turns, allowing LLMs to learn to ask clarifying questions when they can generate tailored responses for each user interpretation [6]. Evaluation on open-domain QA datasets with multiple annotations assesses systems based on their ability to ask clarifying questions to recover each user's interpretation [6]. In educational contexts, frameworks like DCL4KT+LLM predict question difficulties based on text and associated concepts, overcoming missing difficulty information for unseen questions [7]. Additionally, external verifier modules have been proposed to rectify intermediate errors during generation, improving LLM problem-solving performance on challenging math questions [7].

The evaluation of LLM outputs often relies on specific metrics and datasets, such as the percentage of true and informative responses determined by specially trained models [8]. However, most comparisons in some datasets are labeled by only one contractor for cost reasons, which may obscure areas of disagreement among labelers [8]. In the context of prompt engineering, single-stage methods aim to improve the quality of the prompt, while other approaches focus on prompt compression, noting a gap between optimization objectives in these areas [9][10]. Different prompt formats, such as cloze prompts, prefix prompts, and detailed descriptions, are used to activate LLM memory or utilize emergent abilities in downstream tasks [10]. For instance, in QA prompts, few-shot prompts containing specific QA pairs are utilized to guide the model [8]. In LLaMA, the string "Answer these questions:\n" is prepended to the list of questions and answers in all settings [11].

Robustness and security evaluations also play a role in assessing LLM behavior, with benchmarks like AdvBench using prompt suffix attacks and metrics such as Attack Success Rate (ASR) and cross-entropy loss [12]. Tensor Trust evaluates robustness to prompt injection attacks using metrics like Hijacking Extraction Robustness Rate and Defense Validity [12]. While these security-focused evaluations are distinct from clarification efficacy, they highlight the broader empirical landscape in which LLMs are tested. The knowledge boundary of LLMs remains inadequately defined, with limitations in memorization and utilization leading to untruthful responses, which underscores the need for strategies to mitigate these challenges [13]. Incomplete evaluations in areas such as medical questions and long context integration further highlight gaps in current empirical assessments [14].

The primary limitation of interactive clarification systems is the potential for increased user burden and dissatisfaction, particularly when the generated questions are perceived as off-topic or unnecessary. Research indicates that while the need for clarifying questions is sometimes correctly recognized, the questions themselves can be dissatisfaction-provoking and may cause users to leave the conversation [1]. This issue is compounded by the fact that even advanced techniques such as prompt engineering and label words engineering, which are orthogonal to specific tuning methods, do not fully resolve the challenge of maintaining user engagement during complex interactions [2]. Furthermore, from a user perspective, limitations in conversational models like BlenderBot 2.0 have been identified and thoroughly investigated, highlighting the persistent difficulties in aligning model behavior with user expectations [3].

A significant open challenge lies in determining when clarification is necessary versus when the system should proceed with assumptions, a decision that is often complicated by the inherent uncertainty of large language models. The MixAlign framework addresses this by interacting with the user to get clarification specifically when the LLM is uncertain about its mapping from the user query to the database [4]. However, the definition and boundary of each task may not be accurate enough to reliably trigger such clarifications, leading to potential errors in intent detection [5]. In the domain of robotic object disambiguation, few-shot prompt engineering systems have been developed to improve the LLM's ability to pose disambiguating queries, yet the general problem of identifying the precise moment for intervention remains a critical area of research [6].

Latency and computational efficiency are also constrained by the complexity of prompt construction and the gap between optimization objectives. There is a noted gap between optimization objectives in prompt engineering and prompt compression, where the former tends to optimize shorter instructions while the latter deals with longer demonstrations, potentially affecting the speed and efficiency of interactive loops [7]. While automatic prompt engineering significantly alleviates human labor, it still cannot completely avoid human intervention, suggesting that fully autonomous clarification without user input remains an unsolved problem [7]. Additionally, the integration of various advanced techniques, such as prompt pre-training and prompt ensembling, is often left for future work due to simplicity constraints in current implementations, indicating that comprehensive solutions for efficient, interactive prompting are not yet fully realized [2].

The reliability of LLMs in these interactive settings is further challenged by issues of hallucination and consistency. LLMs are prone to hallucination, generating plausible yet nonfactual content, which raises significant concerns over their reliability in real-world applications where accurate intent clarification is crucial [8]. In clinical and medical contexts, the consistency of findings across different evidence levels and prompts varies, with some prompting styles showing higher consistency than others, but overall reliability remains a subject of ongoing assessment [9]. The emergence of LLMs has fueled a paradigm shift in information acquisition, but the phenomenon of hallucination continues to pose a barrier to their deployment in high-stakes decision-making processes that require precise user interaction [8].

Current approaches to handling user intent often rely on specific prompt structures or datasets that may not generalize well. For instance, in some settings, the string "Answer these questions:" is prepended to the list of questions and answers to structure the input, a method that may not be optimal for all interactive scenarios [10]. In the context of source code search, methods for generating clarifying questions have outperformed keyword-based methods for single-turn refinement and were associated with shorter search duration in human studies, suggesting that specific domain adaptations can mitigate some limitations [11]. However, the broader challenge of creating a unified framework for LLM-based autonomous agents that can handle diverse applications and human-like decisions remains, as previous research often focuses on isolated environments that diverge from human learning processes [12].

The integration of human feedback and interactive layers is an active area of development to address these limitations. NesyXIL adds a user interactive layer over existing models to facilitate better interaction, while other systems use human-in-the-loop generation to create adversarial examples for question answering, making the process interactive and model-driven [13][14]. In educational contexts, tools like CodeAid balance student and educator needs by delivering technically correct responses without revealing code solutions, aiming to prevent the hindrance of deep conceptual engagement that can occur with direct answers [15]. Despite these advancements, the field still faces incomplete evaluations in areas such as long context integration and medical questions, indicating that the robustness of interactive clarification systems across diverse domains is not yet fully established [16].
