data.query: Describe what is known about overfitting in in-context learning.

data.answer:
In-context learning (ICL) is defined as a paradigm that allows language models to learn tasks given only a few examples in the form of demonstration, operating on the key idea of learning from analogy [1]. This capability eliminates the need for explicit model retraining or gradient updates, as the model generates responses or performs tasks by inputting cueing examples or related knowledge [2]. ICL can be regarded as a subclass of prompt tuning where the demonstration examples are part of the prompt [1]. However, the performance of ICL is highly sensitive to specific settings, including the prompt template, the selection and order of demonstration examples, and other factors [1]. Consequently, in-context learning is greatly sensitive to the selection of exemplars, and which in-context reasoning examples make the most effective prompts remains an unknown problem in the literature [3][4].

Standard supervised overfitting is characterized by models suffering from increasing validation error as training progresses, such as at epoch 150 when learning rates are reduced [5]. In the context of ICL, overfitting is distinct because it involves the model's inability to effectively utilize labeled samples included in the context [6]. Relying solely on high-confidence data generated from unsupervised downstream tasks for in-context prompting or prompt optimization may lead to overfitting [7]. Furthermore, traditional fine-tuning methods, which are often used to enhance generation quality, are prone to overfitting, degraded generalization, and unnatural language generation [8]. To address these limitations, approaches like Consistent In-Context Editing (ICE) leverage the model's in-context learning capability to optimize toward a contextual distribution rather than a one-hot target, thereby preventing overfitting and preserving the model's integrity [8].

The role of prompt length and the number of demonstrations significantly impacts the generalization ability of ICL. The scarcity of examples poses a challenge to the generalization ability of ICL [1]. Conventional in-context learning is usually restricted by length constraints, rendering it ineffective to absorb supervision from a large number of examples [9]. Enhancing the scalability and efficiency of ICL with more demonstrations remains a significant challenge [1]. While few-shot prompting typically outperforms zero-shot prompting [10], the advent of Long Context Language Models (LCLMs) has raised questions about whether ICL performance in a many-shot regime is still sensitive to the method of sample selection [11]. Surprisingly, sophisticated example selection techniques do not yield significant improvements over a simple random sample selection method in the context of LCLMs [11]. Structured prompting has been introduced to break the length limit and scale in-context learning to thousands of examples by encoding demonstration examples separately with well-designed position embeddings [9].

Theoretical frameworks for understanding ICL often distinguish between memorization and generalization. Transformers exhibit ICL, and recent work shows that the transition from memorization to generalization is sharp with increasing task diversity [12]. One interpretation is that a network's limited capacity to memorize favors generalization, but mechanistic examinations show that the relative rates at which sub-circuits for memorization and generalization learn explains this transition, rather than capacity constraints [12]. A memorization scaling law has been uncovered that determines the task diversity required for this transition [12]. In large language models, distinct neuron subsets are responsible for memorization and generalization behaviors, and inference-time interventions on these neurons can steer the model's behavior toward either [13]. These findings reveal a modular structure in LLMs and enable controlling memorization and generalization behaviors at inference time [13].

Memorization in ICL is closely correlated with performance and the surfacing of training data. ICL significantly surfaces memorization compared to zero-shot learning in most cases [14]. Demonstrations, without their labels, are the most effective element in surfacing memorization [14]. ICL improves performance when the surfaced memorization in few-shot regimes reaches a high level, approximately 40% [14]. There is a very strong correlation between performance and memorization in ICL [14]. However, memorization can also lead to undesirable behaviors, such as the model's output outside the training data [15]. Mixup and CutMix methods reduce the memorization of corrupt labels and facilitate model generalization by averting memorization [15][16]. In the context of pre-training, models attain significantly smaller training losses as the size of the pre-training dataset shrinks, suggesting possible memorization [17]. Deduplication methods have been proposed to simultaneously reduce memorization while improving performance [18].

The sensitivity of ICL to label noise and data quality is evident in its high variance and potential for poor performance. In-context learning performs even worse than manual prompt on some tasks and suffers from high variance [6]. Feature-based methods perform slightly better than manual prompt and in-context learning [6]. ICL methods may be prone to knowledge conflict issues, and their unlearning effectiveness depends on the in-context learning capability of the used LLMs [19]. The debate over whether LLMs genuinely generalize to unseen tasks or predominantly rely on memorizing vast amounts of pretraining data remains active [20]. Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in ICL settings, where models must infer hidden rules behind input prompts without fine-tuning, remains an open and underexplored question [21]. Theoretical surveys aim to unveil the underlying mechanisms of foundation models, covering the analysis of generalization performance [22]. Additionally, in-context deep learning via transformer models provides theoretical guarantees for the approximation and convergence of ICL gradient descent, showing that ICL performance matches that of direct training in synthetic settings [23].

Overfitting in in-context learning (ICL) is characterized by a high sensitivity to specific prompt configurations, including the selection, order, and template of demonstration examples [1][2]. This sensitivity results in high variance in model performance, where ICL can perform even worse than manual prompting on certain tasks [3]. The underlying mechanism involves a failure to effectively utilize the labeled samples included in the context, leading to performance declines that indicate a need for further investigation into these instabilities [3][2]. In few-shot settings, the objective function to be optimized is deterministic rather than stochastic because all training data can be placed into a single batch, which alters the standard bias-variance dynamics observed in stochastic optimization [3]. While the bias-variance tradeoff is a fundamental concept in learning, its application in few-shot scenarios is complicated by the limited number of examples, which remains a major challenge for current models [4][5].

The transition from induction to memorization is a critical mechanism underlying overfitting, as models may rely on memorizing vast amounts of pretraining data rather than genuinely generalizing to unseen tasks [6]. Memorization leads to undesirable behavior outside the training data, a phenomenon that has been observed when models attain significantly smaller training losses as the size of the pre-training dataset shrinks [7][8]. Recent research has identified distinct neuron subsets responsible for memorization versus generalization in Large Language Models (LLMs), demonstrating that these behaviors can be steered at inference time through interventions on specific neurons [9]. This modular structure suggests that LLMs possess the capacity to distinguish between these modes, yet they may still rely on memorization without truly understanding the underlying problems, as seen in domains like molecular chemistry [10]. The debate over whether LLMs generalize or memorize remains active, with some studies failing to find evidence of memorization in complex outputs, though such findings are limited by the unavailability of training sets and models for inspection [11].

Label noise further exacerbates overfitting mechanisms, as deep neural networks have a high capacity to completely memorize noisy labels given sufficient training time, which leads to performance degradation [12]. In practical scenarios, label noise arises from annotator variability and can degrade recognition performance, necessitating methods to identify wrong labels and minimize their negative impact [13]. Regularization techniques, such as early learning regularization, are used to prevent models from overfitting to label noise [14]. Context-based virtual adversarial training (ConVAT) has been proposed to prevent text classifiers from overfitting to noisy labels by enforcing consistency between inputs and perturbed inputs, thereby encouraging the generalization of clean samples while preventing the learning of noisy ones [12]. In federated learning settings, label noise variations among clients can cause existing centralized approaches to exhibit unsatisfactory performance, highlighting the difficulty of handling noisy labels across decentralized training stages [15].

The impact of label noise is also evident in specific application domains, such as audio tagging, where systems must evaluate performance on large sets of noisy-labeled data alongside smaller manually-labeled sets [16]. Similarly, in medical applications like cardiac abnormalities classification, aggregated datasets from various sources are prone to label noise due to inter- and intra-observer variability, which affects the performance and generalizability of trained models [17]. While techniques like Mixup and CutMix can impair baseline performance under certain noise conditions, other regularization strategies aim to improve robustness by interpolating between inputs, although interpolating only between inputs with equal labels does not yield the same performance gains [18][7]. The challenge of learning from very few examples, such as in few-shot class-incremental learning, requires models to preserve the topology of the feature manifold to mitigate forgetting and improve representation learning for new classes [19].

Induction heads in transformers play a role in out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, where models must infer hidden rules behind input prompts without fine-tuning [20]. However, the reliance on memorization can hinder this process, as evidenced by the need for deduplication methods that can simultaneously reduce memorization while improving performance [21]. Metrics such as extraction likelihood and memorization accuracy have been proposed to quantify the extent of memorization by considering overlaps of n-grams and matching of identical token sequences [22]. Despite the potential for overfitting, few-shot learning can achieve cross-lingual capabilities in non-English languages without requiring translation, suggesting that some generalization mechanisms are robust across languages [23]. Furthermore, self-consistency methods can robustly boost performance in few-shot in-context learning for common NLP tasks, offering a reliable way to add rationales and potentially mitigate some instabilities associated with standard prompting [24]. Nevertheless, standard few-shot promptings have not yet proved sufficient to achieve high performance on challenging tasks such as mathematical reasoning, indicating that the mechanisms of overfitting and limited generalization remain significant barriers in complex domains [11].

Empirical investigations into in-context learning (ICL) reveal that the capability to learn from analogy is not uniform and is significantly constrained by the quality and selection of input examples [1]. While ICL is defined as learning from a few examples in the context without explicit model retraining or gradient updates, studies indicate that this mechanism often fails to effectively utilize the labeled samples included in the context [2][1]. Consequently, in-context learning can perform even worse than manual prompting on certain tasks and is characterized by high variance [3]. This instability is further exacerbated by the sensitivity of ICL performance to specific settings, including the prompt template, the selection and order of demonstration examples, and other factors [1]. For instance, despite improvements brought by Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, ICL remains greatly sensitive to the selection of exemplars [4].

The relationship between the number of demonstrations and model performance presents a significant empirical challenge, as enhancing the scalability and efficiency of ICL with more demonstrations remains an open problem [1]. Although ICL can be regarded as a subclass of prompt tuning where demonstration examples are part of the prompt, the ability to rapidly adapt to new tasks and provide human-like responses does not guarantee robustness against overfitting-like behaviors in the context of noisy or poorly selected data [1][5]. Research into noisy label learning provides relevant empirical parallels to these overfitting behaviors, showing that models can suffer from confirmation bias where noisy labels are incorrectly selected as clean, leading to damaged accuracy [6]. In such scenarios, quick convergence to select clean subsets combined with fast overfitting of noisy labels creates an inevitable bias that degrades performance [6].

Comparisons across different learning paradigms and model scales highlight the fragility of ICL compared to other optimization techniques. For example, mixup regularization with a large alpha parameter outperforms dropout on both best and last epoch test errors while remaining resistant to noisy labels, suggesting that standard ICL lacks similar robustness mechanisms [7]. In contrast, ICL’s reliance on input cueing for examples or related knowledge makes it vulnerable to the specific configuration of the prompt rather than the inherent quality of the data distribution [2]. Empirical studies in other domains, such as deep feedforward neural networks for predicting breast cancer metastasis, demonstrate that overfitting tends to negatively correlate with hyperparameters like learning rate, decay, and batch size, indicating that generalization is weakened when models fit too closely to specific training conditions [8]. Similarly, in the context of federated learning, large-scale empirical studies investigating quality from multiple angles of attacks and faults reveal that SOTA techniques face significant quality challenges, mirroring the sensitivity of ICL to environmental and data perturbations [9].

Specific empirical findings on noisy label learning further illustrate the mechanisms of overfitting that parallel ICL's sensitivity to exemplar quality. Methods like Asymmetric Co-teaching (AsyCo) improve over state-of-the-art methods on synthetic and real-world noisy-label datasets by addressing the issue of wrong selection of noisy label samples [6]. However, the underlying problem of overfitting to noisy labels remains a critical factor in model degradation [6]. Furthermore, frameworks like Knockoffs-SPR validate theoretical results through experimental results on benchmark and real-world noisy datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of clean sample selection in mitigating the negative impacts of label noise [10]. These findings collectively suggest that the "overfitting" observed in ICL is closely tied to the model's inability to generalize from the specific, often noisy or suboptimal, set of in-context demonstrations provided [3][6].

Mitigating the overfitting and high variance observed in in-context learning (ICL) involves several strategies, including prompt optimization, ensemble techniques, and careful demonstration selection, though the effectiveness of these methods is often limited by the inherent sensitivity of ICL to exemplar choice [1]. ICL is characterized by a high variance and can perform worse than manual prompting on certain tasks, indicating a susceptibility to overfitting specific context configurations [1]. This sensitivity is further highlighted by the fact that ICL is greatly sensitive to the selection of exemplars, even when using advanced techniques like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting [2]. Consequently, overcoming strong prior biases and ensuring the model gives equal weight to all contextual information remain significant challenges in mitigating this overfitting behavior [3].

Prompt optimization serves as a primary mitigation strategy, with black-box tuning frameworks proposed to optimize continuous prompts via derivative-free optimization [1]. To address the intractability of optimizing in the original high-dimensional prompt space, methods such as black-box tuning perform optimization in a randomly generated subspace, leveraging the low intrinsic dimensionality of large pre-trained models [1]. However, there is a noted gap between optimization objectives in prompt engineering and prompt compression, where the former tends to optimize shorter instructions while the latter deals with longer demonstrations [4]. Despite these optimization efforts, ICL may still suffer from knowledge conflict issues, and the effectiveness of unlearning or mitigation depends on the underlying in-context learning capability of the large language models used [5]. Furthermore, ICL is regarded as a subclass of prompt tuning where demonstration examples are part of the prompt, linking its overfitting characteristics directly to prompt design [3].

Ensemble techniques and self-consistency methods offer another avenue for improving robustness against overfitting. Self-consistency has been shown to be robust to various sampling strategies and parameters, including variations in temperature sampling [6]. This robustness suggests that aggregating multiple reasoning paths can stabilize performance, although the specific application of ensemble methods like bootstrap aggregation (bagging) and cross-validation to reduce overfitting is primarily documented in other domains such as reservoir policy search [7]. In that context, calibration-validation strategies and ensemble aggregation methods were found to improve out-of-sample tradeoffs, providing a methodological parallel for mitigating overfitting in sequential decision-making [7]. Similarly, in portfolio optimization, high out-of-sample performance scores from hold-out techniques can be a "Fata Morgana" arising from vulnerability to overfitting, necessitating dedicated methodologies like combinatorially symmetric cross-validation [8].

Demonstration selection strategies are critical for mitigating overfitting, as they directly influence the ICL performance [3]. Most existing selection strategies operate at the instance level, but the corpus-level selection strategy is considered more important yet remains underexplored [3]. The inability of ICL to effectively utilize labeled samples included in the context further complicates mitigation efforts, as the model may not leverage the provided data to correct for overfitting tendencies [1]. Advanced techniques for ICL have been organized and discussed to address these limitations, but the fundamental issue of sensitivity to exemplar selection persists [2]. While ICL eliminates the need for explicit model retraining or gradient updates by using input cueing, this very mechanism makes the model prone to overfitting the specific context provided [9].

Data augmentation and feature selection techniques, while primarily developed for other domains, offer insights into mitigating overfitting through diverse training samples. For instance, CutMix regularization shows a steady decrease in validation error, indicating that diverse training samples reduce overfitting in classification tasks [10]. In the context of radio galaxy classification, wavelet analysis is used to pick key features and accentuate niche details, aiming to optimize models for high accuracy with fewer features to prevent overfitting caused by new features from powerful telescopes [11]. Additionally, Bayesian methods for tensor networks have been applied to reduce overfitting and improve the performance of normal tensor network models [12]. Although these methods are not directly applied to ICL in the provided evidence, they illustrate the broader principle that reducing feature complexity and increasing sample diversity can mitigate overfitting [11][12][10].

The robustness of ICL is also a key consideration in emerging applications, such as recommendation systems, where an ideal foundation model should demonstrate robust in-context learning capabilities [13]. However, the current state of ICL is hindered by its sensitivity and the challenges in ensuring equal weighting of contextual information, which limits the generalizability of mitigation strategies [3]. The use of few-shot prompts, such as those containing six QA pairs, is a standard practice, but the specific configuration of these prompts can lead to overfitting if not carefully optimized [14]. Ultimately, while prompt optimization, self-consistency, and demonstration selection provide tools to mitigate overfitting, the high variance and sensitivity of ICL to exemplars remain central challenges that require further exploration, particularly at the corpus level [2][1][3].

The fundamental mechanism of in-context learning (ICL) is described as learning from analogy, a process that enables large language models to adapt to new tasks rapidly without explicit model retraining or gradient updates [1][2][3]. However, this capability is not without significant limitations, particularly regarding the effective utilization of labeled samples included in the context, which ICL may fail to leverage effectively [4]. Consequently, the generalization ability of ICL faces challenges due to the scarcity of examples, and the selection of exemplars remains a critical factor, as ICL is greatly sensitive to this choice [5][1]. This sensitivity is further evidenced by observations that ICL can perform worse than manual prompting on certain tasks and suffers from high variance [4].

A major open problem in the literature is determining which in-context reasoning examples constitute the most effective prompts, a question that remains unknown [6]. While standard few-shot prompting provides input–output pairs for test-time examples, this approach has not yet proved sufficient to achieve high performance on challenging tasks such as mathematical reasoning [6]. Similarly, research indicates that models fall short on tasks requiring multiple steps of reasoning, despite their remarkable few-shot performance across other varieties of tasks [7]. The reliance on ICL also introduces risks of knowledge conflict issues, where the effectiveness of unlearning methods depends on the specific ICL capability of the underlying large language models [8].

Theoretical understanding of ICL is currently limited, with explaining ICL through the lens of gradient descent identified as a reasonable, general, and promising direction for future research [1]. ICL is often regarded as a subclass of prompt tuning where demonstration examples are part of the prompt, yet the specific mechanisms driving its success or failure in few-shot settings lack comprehensive theoretical guarantees [1]. To address these gaps, designers are urged to thoroughly explore generalization limitations before integrating models into real-world applications, aiming to maximize transparency of model capabilities [9]. Furthermore, the questions of how emergent abilities arise and whether further scaling will enable additional capabilities remain important future research directions for the field [10].

In summary, while ICL facilitates swift adaptation and human-like responses, the field lacks better metrics to quantify generalization in few-shot settings and robust theoretical frameworks to explain its behavior [3][9]. The high variance and sensitivity to exemplar selection highlight the need for more rigorous analysis of how models process in-context information [5][4]. Future work must continue to address the unknowns regarding optimal prompt construction and the boundaries of ICL's applicability to complex reasoning tasks [6][7].

data.prompt:
You are given a query and a corresponding long answer.

Goal: find irrelevant paragraphs in the answer. These are paragraphs that don't directly answer the query and shouldn't be in the answer.

For instance, if the query is about datasets for scientific question answering, a paragraph about multilingual question answering datasets that don't contain scientific text would be considered irrelevant.

Explicitly consider whether something may be indirectly relevant. For example, if the question is about the conditions of horses in South Africa, a paragraph about general animal welfare in South Africa is potentially relevant while not being precisely about horses. On the other hand, a paragraph about pig welfare in South Africa is irrelevant.

Note that subtle differences can make the text irrelevant to the query. For instance, text about scientific survey paper generation is not relevant to a query about automatic paper review generation. Even though they seem related, they are about very different tasks.

Also, useful background in general is relevant. If the question is about an approach to creating liver-related proteins, some information about liver-related proteins could contextualize other parts of the answer. If a paragraph contextualizes another part of the answer, then it is relevant.

Go through the answer and output a list of irrelevant paragraphs. Every single paragraph needs to be considered, one by one. Our goal is to catch all the irrelevant paragraphs, so please be thorough.
Return your result as a JSON object with a single key `irrelevant_paragraphs` whose value is a list of objects, each having keys `reason`, and `answer_text` as follows:
{"irrelevant_paragraphs":[
{
"reason": "discuss why something is irrelevant (not indirectly relevant)",
"answer_text": "exact ENTIRE paragraph (not just a part of it) from the answer that is irrelevant"
},
...
]
}
Make sure all the irrelevant paragraphs are included.

Context-based virtual adversarial training (ConVAT) has been proposed to prevent text classifiers from overfitting to noisy labels by enforcing consistency between inputs and perturbed inputs, thereby encouraging the generalization of clean samples while preventing the learning of noisy ones [12]. In federated learning settings, label noise variations among clients can cause existing centralized approaches to exhibit unsatisfactory performance, highlighting the difficulty of handling noisy labels across decentralized training stages [15].

The impact of label noise is also evident in specific application domains, such as audio tagging, where systems must evaluate performance on large sets of noisy-labeled data alongside smaller manually-labeled sets [16]. Similarly, in medical applications like cardiac abnormalities classification, aggregated datasets from various sources are prone to label noise due to inter- and intra-observer variability, which affects the performance and generalizability of trained models [17]. While techniques like Mixup and CutMix can impair baseline performance under certain noise conditions, other regularization strategies aim to improve robustness by interpolating between inputs, although interpolating only between inputs with equal labels does not yield the same performance gains [18][7]. The challenge of learning from very few examples, such as in few-shot class-incremental learning, requires models to preserve the topology of the feature manifold to mitigate forgetting and improve representation learning for new classes [19].

Induction heads in transformers play a role in out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, where models must infer hidden rules behind input prompts without fine-tuning [20]. However, the reliance on memorization can hinder this process, as evidenced by the need for deduplication methods that can simultaneously reduce memorization while improving performance [21]. Metrics such as extraction likelihood and memorization accuracy have been proposed to quantify the extent of memorization by considering overlaps of n-grams and matching of identical token sequences [22]. Despite the potential for overfitting, few-shot learning can achieve cross-lingual capabilities in non-English languages without requiring translation, suggesting that some generalization mechanisms are robust across languages [23]. Furthermore, self-consistency methods can robustly boost performance in few-shot in-context learning for common NLP tasks, offering a reliable way to add rationales and potentially mitigate some instabilities associated with standard prompting [24]. Nevertheless, standard few-shot promptings have not yet proved sufficient to achieve high performance on challenging tasks such as mathematical reasoning, indicating that the mechanisms of overfitting and limited generalization remain significant barriers in complex domains [11].

Empirical investigations into in-context learning (ICL) reveal that the capability to learn from analogy is not uniform and is significantly constrained by the quality and selection of input examples [1]. While ICL is defined as learning from a few examples in the context without explicit model retraining or gradient updates, studies indicate that this mechanism often fails to effectively utilize the labeled samples included in the context [2][1]. Consequently, in-context learning can perform even worse than manual prompting on certain tasks and is characterized by high variance [3]. This instability is further exacerbated by the sensitivity of ICL performance to specific settings, including the prompt template, the selection and order of demonstration examples, and other factors [1]. For instance, despite improvements brought by Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, ICL remains greatly sensitive to the selection of exemplars [4].

The relationship between the number of demonstrations and model performance presents a significant empirical challenge, as enhancing the scalability and efficiency of ICL with more demonstrations remains an open problem [1]. Although ICL can be regarded as a subclass of prompt tuning where demonstration examples are part of the prompt, the ability to rapidly adapt to new tasks and provide human-like responses does not guarantee robustness against overfitting-like behaviors in the context of noisy or poorly selected data [1][5]. Research into noisy label learning provides relevant empirical parallels to these overfitting behaviors, showing that models can suffer from confirmation bias where noisy labels are incorrectly selected as clean, leading to damaged accuracy [6]. In such scenarios, quick convergence to select clean subsets combined with fast overfitting of noisy labels creates an inevitable bias that degrades performance [6].

Comparisons across different learning paradigms and model scales highlight the fragility of ICL compared to other optimization techniques. For example, mixup regularization with a large alpha parameter outperforms dropout on both best and last epoch test errors while remaining resistant to noisy labels, suggesting that standard ICL lacks similar robustness mechanisms [7]. In contrast, ICL’s reliance on input cueing for examples or related knowledge makes it vulnerable to the specific configuration of the prompt rather than the inherent quality of the data distribution [2]. Empirical studies in other domains, such as deep feedforward neural networks for predicting breast cancer metastasis, demonstrate that overfitting tends to negatively correlate with hyperparameters like learning rate, decay, and batch size, indicating that generalization is weakened when models fit too closely to specific training conditions [8]. Similarly, in the context of federated learning, large-scale empirical studies investigating quality from multiple angles of attacks and faults reveal that SOTA techniques face significant quality challenges, mirroring the sensitivity of ICL to environmental and data perturbations [9].

Specific empirical findings on noisy label learning further illustrate the mechanisms of overfitting that parallel ICL's sensitivity to exemplar quality. Methods like Asymmetric Co-teaching (AsyCo) improve over state-of-the-art methods on synthetic and real-world noisy-label datasets by addressing the issue of wrong selection of noisy label samples [6]. However, the underlying problem of overfitting to noisy labels remains a critical factor in model degradation [6]. Furthermore, frameworks like Knockoffs-SPR validate theoretical results through experimental results on benchmark and real-world noisy datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of clean sample selection in mitigating the negative impacts of label noise [10]. These findings collectively suggest that the "overfitting" observed in ICL is closely tied to the model's inability to generalize from the specific, often noisy or suboptimal, set of in-context demonstrations provided [3][6].

Mitigating the overfitting and high variance observed in in-context learning (ICL) involves several strategies, including prompt optimization, ensemble techniques, and careful demonstration selection, though the effectiveness of these methods is often limited by the inherent sensitivity of ICL to exemplar choice [1]. ICL is characterized by a high variance and can perform worse than manual prompting on certain tasks, indicating a susceptibility to overfitting specific context configurations [1]. This sensitivity is further highlighted by the fact that ICL is greatly sensitive to the selection of exemplars, even when using advanced techniques like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting [2]. Consequently, overcoming strong prior biases and ensuring the model gives equal weight to all contextual information remain significant challenges in mitigating this overfitting behavior [3].

Prompt optimization serves as a primary mitigation strategy, with black-box tuning frameworks proposed to optimize continuous prompts via derivative-free optimization [1]. To address the intractability of optimizing in the original high-dimensional prompt space, methods such as black-box tuning perform optimization in a randomly generated subspace, leveraging the low intrinsic dimensionality of large pre-trained models [1]. However, there is a noted gap between optimization objectives in prompt engineering and prompt compression, where the former tends to optimize shorter instructions while the latter deals with longer demonstrations [4]. Despite these optimization efforts, ICL may still suffer from knowledge conflict issues, and the effectiveness of unlearning or mitigation depends on the underlying in-context learning capability of the large language models used [5]. Furthermore, ICL is regarded as a subclass of prompt tuning where demonstration examples are part of the prompt, linking its overfitting characteristics directly to prompt design [3].

Ensemble techniques and self-consistency methods offer another avenue for improving robustness against overfitting. Self-consistency has been shown to be robust to various sampling strategies and parameters, including variations in temperature sampling [6]. This robustness suggests that aggregating multiple reasoning paths can stabilize performance, although the specific application of ensemble methods like bootstrap aggregation (bagging) and cross-validation to reduce overfitting is primarily documented in other domains such as reservoir policy search [7]. In that context, calibration-validation strategies and ensemble aggregation methods were found to improve out-of-sample tradeoffs, providing a methodological parallel for mitigating overfitting in sequential decision-making [7]. Similarly, in portfolio optimization, high out-of-sample performance scores from hold-out techniques can be a "Fata Morgana" arising from vulnerability to overfitting, necessitating dedicated methodologies like combinatorially symmetric cross-validation [8].

Demonstration selection strategies are critical for mitigating overfitting, as they directly influence the ICL performance [3]. Most existing selection strategies operate at the instance level, but the corpus-level selection strategy is considered more important yet remains underexplored [3]. The inability of ICL to effectively utilize labeled samples included in the context further complicates mitigation efforts, as the model may not leverage the provided data to correct for overfitting tendencies [1]. Advanced techniques for ICL have been organized and discussed to address these limitations, but the fundamental issue of sensitivity to exemplar selection persists [2]. While ICL eliminates the need for explicit model retraining or gradient updates by using input cueing, this very mechanism makes the model prone to overfitting the specific context provided [9].

Data augmentation and feature selection techniques, while primarily developed for other domains, offer insights into mitigating overfitting through diverse training samples. For instance, CutMix regularization shows a steady decrease in validation error, indicating that diverse training samples reduce overfitting in classification tasks [10]. In the context of radio galaxy classification, wavelet analysis is used to pick key features and accentuate niche details, aiming to optimize models for high accuracy with fewer features to prevent overfitting caused by new features from powerful telescopes [11]. Additionally, Bayesian methods for tensor networks have been applied to reduce overfitting and improve the performance of normal tensor network models [12]. Although these methods are not directly applied to ICL in the provided evidence, they illustrate the broader principle that reducing feature complexity and increasing sample diversity can mitigate overfitting [11][12][10].

The robustness of ICL is also a key consideration in emerging applications, such as recommendation systems, where an ideal foundation model should demonstrate robust in-context learning capabilities [13]. However, the current state of ICL is hindered by its sensitivity and the challenges in ensuring equal weighting of contextual information, which limits the generalizability of mitigation strategies [3]. The use of few-shot prompts, such as those containing six QA pairs, is a standard practice, but the specific configuration of these prompts can lead to overfitting if not carefully optimized [14]. Ultimately, while prompt optimization, self-consistency, and demonstration selection provide tools to mitigate overfitting, the high variance and sensitivity of ICL to exemplars remain central challenges that require further exploration, particularly at the corpus level [2][1][3].

The fundamental mechanism of in-context learning (ICL) is described as learning from analogy, a process that enables large language models to adapt to new tasks rapidly without explicit model retraining or gradient updates [1][2][3]. However, this capability is not without significant limitations, particularly regarding the effective utilization of labeled samples included in the context, which ICL may fail to leverage effectively [4]. Consequently, the generalization ability of ICL faces challenges due to the scarcity of examples, and the selection of exemplars remains a critical factor, as ICL is greatly sensitive to this choice [5][1]. This sensitivity is further evidenced by observations that ICL can perform worse than manual prompting on certain tasks and suffers from high variance [4].

A major open problem in the literature is determining which in-context reasoning examples constitute the most effective prompts, a question that remains unknown [6]. While standard few-shot prompting provides input–output pairs for test-time examples, this approach has not yet proved sufficient to achieve high performance on challenging tasks such as mathematical reasoning [6]. Similarly, research indicates that models fall short on tasks requiring multiple steps of reasoning, despite their remarkable few-shot performance across other varieties of tasks [7]. The reliance on ICL also introduces risks of knowledge conflict issues, where the effectiveness of unlearning methods depends on the specific ICL capability of the underlying large language models [8].

Theoretical understanding of ICL is currently limited, with explaining ICL through the lens of gradient descent identified as a reasonable, general, and promising direction for future research [1]. ICL is often regarded as a subclass of prompt tuning where demonstration examples are part of the prompt, yet the specific mechanisms driving its success or failure in few-shot settings lack comprehensive theoretical guarantees [1]. To address these gaps, designers are urged to thoroughly explore generalization limitations before integrating models into real-world applications, aiming to maximize transparency of model capabilities [9]. Furthermore, the questions of how emergent abilities arise and whether further scaling will enable additional capabilities remain important future research directions for the field [10].

In summary, while ICL facilitates swift adaptation and human-like responses, the field lacks better metrics to quantify generalization in few-shot settings and robust theoretical frameworks to explain its behavior [3][9]. The high variance and sensitivity to exemplar selection highlight the need for more rigorous analysis of how models process in-context information [5][4]. Future work must continue to address the unknowns regarding optimal prompt construction and the boundaries of ICL's applicability to complex reasoning tasks [6][7].

This capability eliminates the need for explicit model retraining or gradient updates, as the model generates responses or performs tasks by inputting cueing examples or related knowledge [2]. ICL can be regarded as a subclass of prompt tuning where the demonstration examples are part of the prompt [1]. However, the performance of ICL is highly sensitive to specific settings, including the prompt template, the selection and order of demonstration examples, and other factors [1]. Consequently, in-context learning is greatly sensitive to the selection of exemplars, and which in-context reasoning examples make the most effective prompts remains an unknown problem in the literature [3][4].

Standard supervised overfitting is characterized by models suffering from increasing validation error as training progresses, such as at epoch 150 when learning rates are reduced [5]. In the context of ICL, overfitting is distinct because it involves the model's inability to effectively utilize labeled samples included in the context [6]. Relying solely on high-confidence data generated from unsupervised downstream tasks for in-context prompting or prompt optimization may lead to overfitting [7]. Furthermore, traditional fine-tuning methods, which are often used to enhance generation quality, are prone to overfitting, degraded generalization, and unnatural language generation [8]. To address these limitations, approaches like Consistent In-Context Editing (ICE) leverage the model's in-context learning capability to optimize toward a contextual distribution rather than a one-hot target, thereby preventing overfitting and preserving the model's integrity [8].

The role of prompt length and the number of demonstrations significantly impacts the generalization ability of ICL. The scarcity of examples poses a challenge to the generalization ability of ICL [1]. Conventional in-context learning is usually restricted by length constraints, rendering it ineffective to absorb supervision from a large number of examples [9]. Enhancing the scalability and efficiency of ICL with more demonstrations remains a significant challenge [1]. While few-shot prompting typically outperforms zero-shot prompting [10], the advent of Long Context Language Models (LCLMs) has raised questions about whether ICL performance in a many-shot regime is still sensitive to the method of sample selection [11]. Surprisingly, sophisticated example selection techniques do not yield significant improvements over a simple random sample selection method in the context of LCLMs [11]. Structured prompting has been introduced to break the length limit and scale in-context learning to thousands of examples by encoding demonstration examples separately with well-designed position embeddings [9].

Theoretical frameworks for understanding ICL often distinguish between memorization and generalization. Transformers exhibit ICL, and recent work shows that the transition from memorization to generalization is sharp with increasing task diversity [12]. One interpretation is that a network's limited capacity to memorize favors generalization, but mechanistic examinations show that the relative rates at which sub-circuits for memorization and generalization learn explains this transition, rather than capacity constraints [12]. A memorization scaling law has been uncovered that determines the task diversity required for this transition [12]. In large language models, distinct neuron subsets are responsible for memorization and generalization behaviors, and inference-time interventions on these neurons can steer the model's behavior toward either [13]. These findings reveal a modular structure in LLMs and enable controlling memorization and generalization behaviors at inference time [13].

Memorization in ICL is closely correlated with performance and the surfacing of training data. ICL significantly surfaces memorization compared to zero-shot learning in most cases [14]. Demonstrations, without their labels, are the most effective element in surfacing memorization [14]. ICL improves performance when the surfaced memorization in few-shot regimes reaches a high level, approximately 40% [14]. There is a very strong correlation between performance and memorization in ICL [14]. However, memorization can also lead to undesirable behaviors, such as the model's output outside the training data [15]. Mixup and CutMix methods reduce the memorization of corrupt labels and facilitate model generalization by averting memorization [15][16]. In the context of pre-training, models attain significantly smaller training losses as the size of the pre-training dataset shrinks, suggesting possible memorization [17]. Deduplication methods have been proposed to simultaneously reduce memorization while improving performance [18].

The sensitivity of ICL to label noise and data quality is evident in its high variance and potential for poor performance. In-context learning performs even worse than manual prompt on some tasks and suffers from high variance [6]. Feature-based methods perform slightly better than manual prompt and in-context learning [6]. ICL methods may be prone to knowledge conflict issues, and their unlearning effectiveness depends on the in-context learning capability of the used LLMs [19]. The debate over whether LLMs genuinely generalize to unseen tasks or predominantly rely on memorizing vast amounts of pretraining data remains active [20]. Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in ICL settings, where models must infer hidden rules behind input prompts without fine-tuning, remains an open and underexplored question [21]. Theoretical surveys aim to unveil the underlying mechanisms of foundation models, covering the analysis of generalization performance [22]. Additionally, in-context deep learning via transformer models provides theoretical guarantees for the approximation and convergence of ICL gradient descent, showing that ICL performance matches that of direct training in synthetic settings [23].

However, this capability is not without significant limitations, particularly regarding the effective utilization of labeled samples included in the context, which ICL may fail to leverage effectively [4]. Consequently, the generalization ability of ICL faces challenges due to the scarcity of examples, and the selection of exemplars remains a critical factor, as ICL is greatly sensitive to this choice [5][1]. While standard few-shot prompting provides input–output pairs for test-time examples, this approach has not yet proved sufficient to achieve high performance on challenging tasks such as mathematical reasoning [6]. Similarly, research indicates that models fall short on tasks requiring multiple steps of reasoning, despite their remarkable few-shot performance across other varieties of tasks [7]. The reliance on ICL also introduces risks of knowledge conflict issues, where the effectiveness of unlearning methods depends on the specific ICL capability of the underlying large language models [8].

Theoretical understanding of ICL is currently limited, with explaining ICL through the lens of gradient descent identified as a reasonable, general, and promising direction for future research [1]. ICL is often regarded as a subclass of prompt tuning where demonstration examples are part of the prompt, yet the specific mechanisms driving its success or failure in few-shot settings lack comprehensive theoretical guarantees [1]. To address these gaps, designers are urged to thoroughly explore generalization limitations before integrating models into real-world applications, aiming to maximize transparency of model capabilities [9]. Furthermore, the questions of how emergent abilities arise and whether further scaling will enable additional capabilities remain important future research directions for the field [10].

In summary, while ICL facilitates swift adaptation and human-like responses, the field lacks better metrics to quantify generalization in few-shot settings and robust theoretical frameworks to explain its behavior [3][9]. The high variance and sensitivity to exemplar selection highlight the need for more rigorous analysis of how models process in-context information [5][4]. Future work must continue to address the unknowns regarding optimal prompt construction and the boundaries of ICL's applicability to complex reasoning tasks [6][7].

In-context learning (ICL) is defined as a paradigm that allows language models to learn tasks given only a few examples in the form of demonstration, operating on the key idea of learning from analogy [1]. This capability eliminates the need for explicit model retraining or gradient updates, as the model generates responses or performs tasks by inputting cueing examples or related knowledge [2]. ICL can be regarded as a subclass of prompt tuning where the demonstration examples are part of the prompt [1]. However, the performance of ICL is highly sensitive to specific settings, including the prompt template, the selection and order of demonstration examples, and other factors [1]. Consequently, in-context learning is greatly sensitive to the selection of exemplars, and which in-context reasoning examples make the most effective prompts remains an unknown problem in the literature [3][4].

Standard supervised overfitting is characterized by models suffering from increasing validation error as training progresses, such as at epoch 150 when learning rates are reduced [5]. In the context of ICL, overfitting is distinct because it involves the model's inability to effectively utilize labeled samples included in the context [6]. Relying solely on high-confidence data generated from unsupervised downstream tasks for in-context prompting or prompt optimization may lead to overfitting [7]. Furthermore, traditional fine-tuning methods, which are often used to enhance generation quality, are prone to overfitting, degraded generalization, and unnatural language generation [8]. To address these limitations, approaches like Consistent In-Context Editing (ICE) leverage the model's in-context learning capability to optimize toward a contextual distribution rather than a one-hot target, thereby preventing overfitting and preserving the model's integrity [8].

The role of prompt length and the number of demonstrations significantly impacts the generalization ability of ICL. The scarcity of examples poses a challenge to the generalization ability of ICL [1]. Conventional in-context learning is usually restricted by length constraints, rendering it ineffective to absorb supervision from a large number of examples [9]. Enhancing the scalability and efficiency of ICL with more demonstrations remains a significant challenge [1]. While few-shot prompting typically outperforms zero-shot prompting [10], the advent of Long Context Language Models (LCLMs) has raised questions about whether ICL performance in a many-shot regime is still sensitive to the method of sample selection [11]. Surprisingly, sophisticated example selection techniques do not yield significant improvements over a simple random sample selection method in the context of LCLMs [11]. Structured prompting has been introduced to break the length limit and scale in-context learning to thousands of examples by encoding demonstration examples separately with well-designed position embeddings [9].

Theoretical frameworks for understanding ICL often distinguish between memorization and generalization. Transformers exhibit ICL, and recent work shows that the transition from memorization to generalization is sharp with increasing task diversity [12]. One interpretation is that a network's limited capacity to memorize favors generalization, but mechanistic examinations show that the relative rates at which sub-circuits for memorization and generalization learn explains this transition, rather than capacity constraints [12]. A memorization scaling law has been uncovered that determines the task diversity required for this transition [12]. In large language models, distinct neuron subsets are responsible for memorization and generalization behaviors, and inference-time interventions on these neurons can steer the model's behavior toward either [13]. These findings reveal a modular structure in LLMs and enable controlling memorization and generalization behaviors at inference time [13].

Memorization in ICL is closely correlated with performance and the surfacing of training data. ICL significantly surfaces memorization compared to zero-shot learning in most cases [14]. Demonstrations, without their labels, are the most effective element in surfacing memorization [14]. ICL improves performance when the surfaced memorization in few-shot regimes reaches a high level, approximately 40% [14]. There is a very strong correlation between performance and memorization in ICL [14]. However, memorization can also lead to undesirable behaviors, such as the model's output outside the training data [15]. Mixup and CutMix methods reduce the memorization of corrupt labels and facilitate model generalization by averting memorization [15][16]. In the context of pre-training, models attain significantly smaller training losses as the size of the pre-training dataset shrinks, suggesting possible memorization [17]. Deduplication methods have been proposed to simultaneously reduce memorization while improving performance [18].

The sensitivity of ICL to label noise and data quality is evident in its high variance and potential for poor performance. In-context learning performs even worse than manual prompt on some tasks and suffers from high variance [6]. Feature-based methods perform slightly better than manual prompt and in-context learning [6]. ICL methods may be prone to knowledge conflict issues, and their unlearning effectiveness depends on the in-context learning capability of the used LLMs [19]. The debate over whether LLMs genuinely generalize to unseen tasks or predominantly rely on memorizing vast amounts of pretraining data remains active [20]. Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in ICL settings, where models must infer hidden rules behind input prompts without fine-tuning, remains an open and underexplored question [21]. Theoretical surveys aim to unveil the underlying mechanisms of foundation models, covering the analysis of generalization performance [22]. Additionally, in-context deep learning via transformer models provides theoretical guarantees for the approximation and convergence of ICL gradient descent, showing that ICL performance matches that of direct training in synthetic settings [23].

Overfitting in in-context learning (ICL) is characterized by a high sensitivity to specific prompt configurations, including the selection, order, and template of demonstration examples [1][2]. This sensitivity results in high variance in model performance, where ICL can perform even worse than manual prompting on certain tasks [3]. The underlying mechanism involves a failure to effectively utilize the labeled samples included in the context, leading to performance declines that indicate a need for further investigation into these instabilities [3][2]. In few-shot settings, the objective function to be optimized is deterministic rather than stochastic because all training data can be placed into a single batch, which alters the standard bias-variance dynamics observed in stochastic optimization [3]. While the bias-variance tradeoff is a fundamental concept in learning, its application in few-shot scenarios is complicated by the limited number of examples, which remains a major challenge for current models [4][5].

The transition from induction to memorization is a critical mechanism underlying overfitting, as models may rely on memorizing vast amounts of pretraining data rather than genuinely generalizing to unseen tasks [6]. Memorization leads to undesirable behavior outside the training data, a phenomenon that has been observed when models attain significantly smaller training losses as the size of the pre-training dataset shrinks [7][8]. Recent research has identified distinct neuron subsets responsible for memorization versus generalization in Large Language Models (LLMs), demonstrating that these behaviors can be steered at inference time through interventions on specific neurons [9]. This modular structure suggests that LLMs possess the capacity to distinguish between these modes, yet they may still rely on memorization without truly understanding the underlying problems, as seen in domains like molecular chemistry [10]. The debate over whether LLMs generalize or memorize remains active, with some studies failing to find evidence of memorization in complex outputs, though such findings are limited by the unavailability of training sets and models for inspection [11].

Label noise further exacerbates overfitting mechanisms, as deep neural networks have a high capacity to completely memorize noisy labels given sufficient training time, which leads to performance degradation [12]. In practical scenarios, label noise arises from annotator variability and can degrade recognition performance, necessitating methods to identify wrong labels and minimize their negative impact [13]. Regularization techniques, such as early learning regularization, are used to prevent models from overfitting to label noise [14]. Context-based virtual adversarial training (ConVAT) has been proposed to prevent text classifiers from overfitting to noisy labels by enforcing consistency between inputs and perturbed inputs, thereby encouraging the generalization of clean samples while preventing the learning of noisy ones [12]. In federated learning settings, label noise variations among clients can cause existing centralized approaches to exhibit unsatisfactory performance, highlighting the difficulty of handling noisy labels across decentralized training stages [15].

The impact of label noise is also evident in specific application domains, such as audio tagging, where systems must evaluate performance on large sets of noisy-labeled data alongside smaller manually-labeled sets [16]. Similarly, in medical applications like cardiac abnormalities classification, aggregated datasets from various sources are prone to label noise due to inter- and intra-observer variability, which affects the performance and generalizability of trained models [17]. While techniques like Mixup and CutMix can impair baseline performance under certain noise conditions, other regularization strategies aim to improve robustness by interpolating between inputs, although interpolating only between inputs with equal labels does not yield the same performance gains [18][7]. The challenge of learning from very few examples, such as in few-shot class-incremental learning, requires models to preserve the topology of the feature manifold to mitigate forgetting and improve representation learning for new classes [19].

Induction heads in transformers play a role in out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, where models must infer hidden rules behind input prompts without fine-tuning [20]. However, the reliance on memorization can hinder this process, as evidenced by the need for deduplication methods that can simultaneously reduce memorization while improving performance [21]. Metrics such as extraction likelihood and memorization accuracy have been proposed to quantify the extent of memorization by considering overlaps of n-grams and matching of identical token sequences [22]. Despite the potential for overfitting, few-shot learning can achieve cross-lingual capabilities in non-English languages without requiring translation, suggesting that some generalization mechanisms are robust across languages [23]. Furthermore, self-consistency methods can robustly boost performance in few-shot in-context learning for common NLP tasks, offering a reliable way to add rationales and potentially mitigate some instabilities associated with standard prompting [24]. Nevertheless, standard few-shot promptings have not yet proved sufficient to achieve high performance on challenging tasks such as mathematical reasoning, indicating that the mechanisms of overfitting and limited generalization remain significant barriers in complex domains [11].

Empirical investigations into in-context learning (ICL) reveal that the capability to learn from analogy is not uniform and is significantly constrained by the quality and selection of input examples [1]. While ICL is defined as learning from a few examples in the context without explicit model retraining or gradient updates, studies indicate that this mechanism often fails to effectively utilize the labeled samples included in the context [2][1]. Consequently, in-context learning can perform even worse than manual prompting on certain tasks and is characterized by high variance [3]. This instability is further exacerbated by the sensitivity of ICL performance to specific settings, including the prompt template, the selection and order of demonstration examples, and other factors [1]. For instance, despite improvements brought by Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, ICL remains greatly sensitive to the selection of exemplars [4].

The relationship between the number of demonstrations and model performance presents a significant empirical challenge, as enhancing the scalability and efficiency of ICL with more demonstrations remains an open problem [1]. Although ICL can be regarded as a subclass of prompt tuning where demonstration examples are part of the prompt, the ability to rapidly adapt to new tasks and provide human-like responses does not guarantee robustness against overfitting-like behaviors in the context of noisy or poorly selected data [1][5]. Research into noisy label learning provides relevant empirical parallels to these overfitting behaviors, showing that models can suffer from confirmation bias where noisy labels are incorrectly selected as clean, leading to damaged accuracy [6]. In such scenarios, quick convergence to select clean subsets combined with fast overfitting of noisy labels creates an inevitable bias that degrades performance [6].

Comparisons across different learning paradigms and model scales highlight the fragility of ICL compared to other optimization techniques. For example, mixup regularization with a large alpha parameter outperforms dropout on both best and last epoch test errors while remaining resistant to noisy labels, suggesting that standard ICL lacks similar robustness mechanisms [7]. In contrast, ICL’s reliance on input cueing for examples or related knowledge makes it vulnerable to the specific configuration of the prompt rather than the inherent quality of the data distribution [2]. Empirical studies in other domains, such as deep feedforward neural networks for predicting breast cancer metastasis, demonstrate that overfitting tends to negatively correlate with hyperparameters like learning rate, decay, and batch size, indicating that generalization is weakened when models fit too closely to specific training conditions [8]. Similarly, in the context of federated learning, large-scale empirical studies investigating quality from multiple angles of attacks and faults reveal that SOTA techniques face significant quality challenges, mirroring the sensitivity of ICL to environmental and data perturbations [9].

Specific empirical findings on noisy label learning further illustrate the mechanisms of overfitting that parallel ICL's sensitivity to exemplar quality. Methods like Asymmetric Co-teaching (AsyCo) improve over state-of-the-art methods on synthetic and real-world noisy-label datasets by addressing the issue of wrong selection of noisy label samples [6]. However, the underlying problem of overfitting to noisy labels remains a critical factor in model degradation [6]. Furthermore, frameworks like Knockoffs-SPR validate theoretical results through experimental results on benchmark and real-world noisy datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of clean sample selection in mitigating the negative impacts of label noise [10]. These findings collectively suggest that the "overfitting" observed in ICL is closely tied to the model's inability to generalize from the specific, often noisy or suboptimal, set of in-context demonstrations provided [3][6].

Mitigating the overfitting and high variance observed in in-context learning (ICL) involves several strategies, including prompt optimization, ensemble techniques, and careful demonstration selection, though the effectiveness of these methods is often limited by the inherent sensitivity of ICL to exemplar choice [1]. ICL is characterized by a high variance and can perform worse than manual prompting on certain tasks, indicating a susceptibility to overfitting specific context configurations [1]. This sensitivity is further highlighted by the fact that ICL is greatly sensitive to the selection of exemplars, even when using advanced techniques like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting [2]. Consequently, overcoming strong prior biases and ensuring the model gives equal weight to all contextual information remain significant challenges in mitigating this overfitting behavior [3].

Prompt optimization serves as a primary mitigation strategy, with black-box tuning frameworks proposed to optimize continuous prompts via derivative-free optimization [1]. To address the intractability of optimizing in the original high-dimensional prompt space, methods such as black-box tuning perform optimization in a randomly generated subspace, leveraging the low intrinsic dimensionality of large pre-trained models [1]. However, there is a noted gap between optimization objectives in prompt engineering and prompt compression, where the former tends to optimize shorter instructions while the latter deals with longer demonstrations [4]. Despite these optimization efforts, ICL may still suffer from knowledge conflict issues, and the effectiveness of unlearning or mitigation depends on the underlying in-context learning capability of the large language models used [5]. Furthermore, ICL is regarded as a subclass of prompt tuning where demonstration examples are part of the prompt, linking its overfitting characteristics directly to prompt design [3].

Ensemble techniques and self-consistency methods offer another avenue for improving robustness against overfitting. Self-consistency has been shown to be robust to various sampling strategies and parameters, including variations in temperature sampling [6]. This robustness suggests that aggregating multiple reasoning paths can stabilize performance, although the specific application of ensemble methods like bootstrap aggregation (bagging) and cross-validation to reduce overfitting is primarily documented in other domains such as reservoir policy search [7]. In that context, calibration-validation strategies and ensemble aggregation methods were found to improve out-of-sample tradeoffs, providing a methodological parallel for mitigating overfitting in sequential decision-making [7]. Similarly, in portfolio optimization, high out-of-sample performance scores from hold-out techniques can be a "Fata Morgana" arising from vulnerability to overfitting, necessitating dedicated methodologies like combinatorially symmetric cross-validation [8].

Demonstration selection strategies are critical for mitigating overfitting, as they directly influence the ICL performance [3]. Most existing selection strategies operate at the instance level, but the corpus-level selection strategy is considered more important yet remains underexplored [3]. The inability of ICL to effectively utilize labeled samples included in the context further complicates mitigation efforts, as the model may not leverage the provided data to correct for overfitting tendencies [1]. Advanced techniques for ICL have been organized and discussed to address these limitations, but the fundamental issue of sensitivity to exemplar selection persists [2]. While ICL eliminates the need for explicit model retraining or gradient updates by using input cueing, this very mechanism makes the model prone to overfitting the specific context provided [9].

For instance, CutMix regularization shows a steady decrease in validation error, indicating that diverse training samples reduce overfitting in classification tasks [10]. Additionally, Bayesian methods for tensor networks have been applied to reduce overfitting and improve the performance of normal tensor network models [12]. Although these methods are not directly applied to ICL in the provided evidence, they illustrate the broader principle that reducing feature complexity and increasing sample diversity can mitigate overfitting [11][12][10].

The robustness of ICL is also a key consideration in emerging applications, such as recommendation systems, where an ideal foundation model should demonstrate robust in-context learning capabilities [13]. However, the current state of ICL is hindered by its sensitivity and the challenges in ensuring equal weighting of contextual information, which limits the generalizability of mitigation strategies [3]. The use of few-shot prompts, such as those containing six QA pairs, is a standard practice, but the specific configuration of these prompts can lead to overfitting if not carefully optimized [14]. Ultimately, while prompt optimization, self-consistency, and demonstration selection provide tools to mitigate overfitting, the high variance and sensitivity of ICL to exemplars remain central challenges that require further exploration, particularly at the corpus level [2][1][3].

You are a claim validator. For each claim made in the following text you will determine if it is supported by the quote from it's corresponding inline citations. As is typically done in academic writing, assume that consecutive sentences can share citations. Make sure to also include claims presented in table format. For references with only the title available (ie no quotes from the reference are included), judge them as `supporting` if the title indicates that the paper is likely relevant to the claim being considered. Return a JSON object with a single key `claims` which is a list of `claim` objects, one for each sentence in the text. Each `claim` object contains the claim itself (`text`), a list of `supporting` inline citations and `non_supporting` inline citations and finally a boolean `is_fully_supported` which indicates if the claim is entirely supported by the quotations in the associated citations. Each inline citation corresponding to that claim should appear in either `supporting` or `non_supporting`, but not both. Each claim made in the text should appear in your output, but you should skip sentences covering high level introductory information.

Text:
In-context learning (ICL) is defined as a paradigm that allows language models to learn tasks given only a few examples in the form of demonstration, operating on the key idea of learning from analogy [1]. This capability eliminates the need for explicit model retraining or gradient updates, as the model generates responses or performs tasks by inputting cueing examples or related knowledge [2]. ICL can be regarded as a subclass of prompt tuning where the demonstration examples are part of the prompt [1]. However, the performance of ICL is highly sensitive to specific settings, including the prompt template, the selection and order of demonstration examples, and other factors [1]. Consequently, in-context learning is greatly sensitive to the selection of exemplars, and which in-context reasoning examples make the most effective prompts remains an unknown problem in the literature [3][4].

Standard supervised overfitting is characterized by models suffering from increasing validation error as training progresses, such as at epoch 150 when learning rates are reduced [5]. In the context of ICL, overfitting is distinct because it involves the model's inability to effectively utilize labeled samples included in the context [6]. Relying solely on high-confidence data generated from unsupervised downstream tasks for in-context prompting or prompt optimization may lead to overfitting [7]. Furthermore, traditional fine-tuning methods, which are often used to enhance generation quality, are prone to overfitting, degraded generalization, and unnatural language generation [8]. To address these limitations, approaches like Consistent In-Context Editing (ICE) leverage the model's in-context learning capability to optimize toward a contextual distribution rather than a one-hot target, thereby preventing overfitting and preserving the model's integrity [8].

The role of prompt length and the number of demonstrations significantly impacts the generalization ability of ICL. The scarcity of examples poses a challenge to the generalization ability of ICL [1]. Conventional in-context learning is usually restricted by length constraints, rendering it ineffective to absorb supervision from a large number of examples [9]. Enhancing the scalability and efficiency of ICL with more demonstrations remains a significant challenge [1]. While few-shot prompting typically outperforms zero-shot prompting [10], the advent of Long Context Language Models (LCLMs) has raised questions about whether ICL performance in a many-shot regime is still sensitive to the method of sample selection [11]. Surprisingly, sophisticated example selection techniques do not yield significant improvements over a simple random sample selection method in the context of LCLMs [11]. Structured prompting has been introduced to break the length limit and scale in-context learning to thousands of examples by encoding demonstration examples separately with well-designed position embeddings [9].

Theoretical frameworks for understanding ICL often distinguish between memorization and generalization. Transformers exhibit ICL, and recent work shows that the transition from memorization to generalization is sharp with increasing task diversity [12]. One interpretation is that a network's limited capacity to memorize favors generalization, but mechanistic examinations show that the relative rates at which sub-circuits for memorization and generalization learn explains this transition, rather than capacity constraints [12]. A memorization scaling law has been uncovered that determines the task diversity required for this transition [12]. In large language models, distinct neuron subsets are responsible for memorization and generalization behaviors, and inference-time interventions on these neurons can steer the model's behavior toward either [13]. These findings reveal a modular structure in LLMs and enable controlling memorization and generalization behaviors at inference time [13].

Memorization in ICL is closely correlated with performance and the surfacing of training data. ICL significantly surfaces memorization compared to zero-shot learning in most cases [14]. Demonstrations, without their labels, are the most effective element in surfacing memorization [14]. ICL improves performance when the surfaced memorization in few-shot regimes reaches a high level, approximately 40% [14]. There is a very strong correlation between performance and memorization in ICL [14]. However, memorization can also lead to undesirable behaviors, such as the model's output outside the training data [15]. Mixup and CutMix methods reduce the memorization of corrupt labels and facilitate model generalization by averting memorization [15][16]. In the context of pre-training, models attain significantly smaller training losses as the size of the pre-training dataset shrinks, suggesting possible memorization [17]. Deduplication methods have been proposed to simultaneously reduce memorization while improving performance [18].

The sensitivity of ICL to label noise and data quality is evident in its high variance and potential for poor performance. In-context learning performs even worse than manual prompt on some tasks and suffers from high variance [6]. Feature-based methods perform slightly better than manual prompt and in-context learning [6]. ICL methods may be prone to knowledge conflict issues, and their unlearning effectiveness depends on the in-context learning capability of the used LLMs [19]. The debate over whether LLMs genuinely generalize to unseen tasks or predominantly rely on memorizing vast amounts of pretraining data remains active [20]. Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in ICL settings, where models must infer hidden rules behind input prompts without fine-tuning, remains an open and underexplored question [21]. Theoretical surveys aim to unveil the underlying mechanisms of foundation models, covering the analysis of generalization performance [22]. Additionally, in-context deep learning via transformer models provides theoretical guarantees for the approximation and convergence of ICL gradient descent, showing that ICL performance matches that of direct training in synthetic settings [23].
